chunks: From him, from Ahmad, from al-Husayn, from Fudaylah, from Aban ibn 'Uthman, from al-Fadl ibn 'Abd al-Malik, who said:

I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the travelers who differ [in their practice of shortening prayers], so he said, 'When they hasten the journey, they should shorten [the prayers].' The resolution between these two narrations is what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Kulayni mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him, who said: 'This is to be understood as referring to one who considers two stations as one station, so he shortens [the prayer] on the road and completes [it] at the station. And that which reveals this is what he narrated...'

key_terms.الْمَنْزِلَيْنِ: The two stations (stops or resting places)
key_terms.الْمُكَارِينَ: Travelers who make multiple stops or have varying travel schedules
key_terms.لْيَقْصُرُوا: They should shorten (the four-rak'ah prayers to two)
key_terms.وَيُتِمُّ: And he completes (the prayer to four rak'ahs)
key_terms.يَخْتَلِفُونَ: They differ (in legal practice or opinion)

ai.seo_question: How should travelers shorten their prayers if they have different practices regarding journey duration?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the practical application of *qasr* (shortening prayers) by linking it to the traveler's pace, specifically those who 'hasten' their journey. The apparent contradiction with other reports is resolved through the principle of *jam'* (combining stations), where a traveler treating multiple stops as one residence completes prayers there, whereas those moving continuously shorten them. This reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on the traveler's actual state of movement versus settlement in determining ritual obligations.
